pattern.notes: Each question carries 1.25 marks and there is no negative marking. 10 extra minutes are given to read instructions. The real Mental Ability section is entirely figure-based (10 parts × 4 questions). The mock renders these as figure questions (inline SVG problem and answer figures). The Language test uses 4 passages × 5 questions; here passages are repeated inside each question.

trendAnalysis.summary: Based on the 2024 paper and the two-phase 2025 and 2026 tests. The pattern has been fixed since 2020: Mental Ability (50%) decides the merit, with odd-one-out, figure series, mirror imaging, punched-hole and embedded-figure items of easy to moderate level. Arithmetic covers the Class 5 syllabus, with number system, fractions/decimals, measurement, percentage/profit-loss and area-perimeter being the high-yield topics; recent papers favour short word problems over plain computation. The Language test has four easy factual passages, with occasional vocabulary-in-context and title questions. Overall difficulty is easy to moderate; speed and accuracy in Mental Ability matter most.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the JNVST 2024 paper and the Phase-1/Phase-2 papers of JNVST 2025 and 2026 as reproduced in unofficial answer keys and solved-paper compilations (Careers360 answer-key pages, Arihant solved papers; found via web search, Oct 2026) and the writer's own knowledge of these papers. Official NVS papers could not be fetched. The real Mental Ability Test is figure-based (10 parts × 4); each archetype describes the figure format; the mock renders these items as figure questions with inline SVG drawings.

archetypes.pattern: Four answer figures: three are the same figure turned through 90°/180°/270°, one is its mirror image (or has one element on the other side) – pick the odd figure
Odd figure by a counting/shape property: number of dots or lines vs number of sides, inner shape same as outer shape, open vs closed figure
One problem figure; pick the exact copy among four near-identical figures that differ in one detail (direction of a line, position of a dot or small shape)
Composite design with several small marks; distractors are the same design turned, mirror-reversed or with two marks swapped – pick the identical one
Symmetric square design with one quarter missing (marked ?); pick the quarter that continues the lines, arcs and dots
Line design with a small square cut out; pick the piece whose line segments continue the lines/curves across the gap (distractors mirrored, turned or missing a line)
Three or four problem figures where elements are added (sides, shaded parts, arrows) and/or a feature alternates; pick the next figure
An element turns by a fixed angle (45°/90°) and/or a small mark moves corner to corner each step; pick the next figure (mirror-image distractor)
A : B :: C : ? where B is A turned (90°/180°) or mirror-reversed; apply the same change to C
A : B :: C : ? where B swaps inner and outer shapes, reverses shading or changes the number of elements; apply the same change to C
Each answer figure shows 2–3 separate pieces; pick the one whose pieces can be joined (turning allowed) to make a complete square
A square with one piece missing; pick the piece of the right shape and size that completes it (distractors mirrored or wrongly sized)
Mirror image of a figure or a group of letters/digits in a vertical mirror (line MN at the side): left–right reversed, order reversed
Water image (mirror line MN below) of a figure or character group: top–bottom reversed, order kept; distractors are the vertical-mirror image or a half turn
Square sheet folded once or twice along the middle lines, punched; pick the unfolded sheet (holes double with each fold, at mirror positions)
Diagonal fold or holes of different shapes; pick the unfolded sheet with each hole at its mirror position across the fold (translation distractors)
A complete figure is given; pick the answer figure showing the set of pieces (correct shapes, sizes and number) from which it can be made
Separate pieces are given; pick the figure they form when joined (distractors with wrong proportions)
A simple figure X is given; pick the complex answer figure in which X is hidden in the same size and direction (distractors contain its mirror image, a turned or a bigger copy)
Reverse form: a complex problem figure is given; pick the simple answer figure hidden in it in the same size and direction
Place value/face value, expanded form, comparison of large numbers
Form the smallest/largest number from given digits; Roman numerals; even/odd and prime facts
LCM/HCF of small numbers, often as a word problem (bells, remainder, greatest length)
Add/subtract fractions in a word problem ('what fraction is left'); compare fractions
Decimal multiplication/division with place-value traps (0.01 vs 0.1)
Multi-step word problem with ×, ÷, +, − (boxes, items, money)
Percentage of a quantity or the complementary part (boys/girls, pass/fail)
Profit/loss and profit/loss per cent from CP and SP
SI, rate or time using SI = P × R × T / 100
Distance = speed × time with hours/minutes, or same speed for a new distance
Unit conversion and addition of compound units (km–m, kg–g, L–mL)
Time duration between two clock times / hours–minutes conversion
Perimeter/area of squares and rectangles, including tiles needed or equal perimeters
Volume of cube/cuboid
Angles of triangles, clock-hand turning, right/straight angles
Properties of shapes: sides, vertices, diagonals
Direct-detail question (who/what/where) answered by one sentence of a short passage
'Why' question whose answer is a stated reason in the passage; distractors are details from other sentences
Meaning of a word/phrase as used in the passage
Synonym/opposite of a word taken from the passage
Most suitable title for the passage
Inference: quality of a character, main idea or lesson of the passage

Passage: Sundarpur was a small village with a big pond at its centre. Every summer the pond dried up, and the women had to walk three kilometres to fetch water. One year, the school teacher, Mr. Rao, asked the children to help. Together with their parents, they cleaned the pond, removed the plastic waste and dug small channels so that rainwater from the fields would flow into it. When the monsoon came, the pond filled to the brim. By the next summer there was still water in it, and the women no longer had to walk far. The villagers decided to celebrate 'Pond Day' every year.

Question: Why did the women have to walk three kilometres in summer?
options: Because the pond was very dirty
Because they wanted to meet friends
Because the teacher told them to
questions.explanation: The passage says that every summer the pond dried up, so the women had to fetch water from three kilometres away.

relevance.note: Stated reason (pond dried up) with 'dirty pond' near-miss; JNVST RC style

Passage: Arjun lived in a village at the edge of a forest. Every morning he took his family's goats to graze on the hillside. One hot afternoon he noticed smoke rising from the dry grass near the forest. He knew that even a small fire could spread quickly in the strong summer wind. He worked at the forest office
He took the goats to graze on the hillside
questions.explanation: The passage says that every morning he took his family's goats to graze on the hillside.

relevance.note: Daily routine detail; direct factual

Passage: The camel is well suited to life in the desert. Its long legs keep its body away from the hot sand, and its broad, padded feet do not sink into it. Passage: Paper is made from wood pulp, so every sheet we waste means that more trees have to be cut. Old newspapers, notebooks and cartons can be recycled. At a recycling unit, used paper is first soaked in water and beaten into a soft pulp. The ink is washed away, and the clean pulp is pressed and dried into new sheets. Making paper in this way uses less water and energy than making it from fresh wood. Students can help by writing on both sides of a page, using old calendars as book covers and keeping waste paper separate from wet kitchen waste.

Passage: Paper is made from wood pulp, so every sheet we waste means that more trees have to be cut. Old newspapers, notebooks and cartons can be recycled. At a recycling unit, used paper is first soaked in water and beaten into a soft pulp. The ink is washed away, and the clean pulp is pressed and dried into new sheets.
